title: BURTON v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary:
In Burton v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Ms. Burton, is a British citizen of Romany Gypsy origin residing in Carmarthen, Wales. Her case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities, particularly regarding the right to maintain their traditional way of life in the face of restrictive local authority policies and planning laws. After years of living in settled accommodation due to repeated evictions and the absence of permanent caravan sites, Ms. Burton, diagnosed with terminal cancer, wished to spend her final days in a caravan according to Romany Gypsy tradition. Despite her family's efforts to secure a lawful site for their caravan, the local council was unable to provide suitable accommodation, and requests to live in a council-owned mobile home were refused.

Ms. Burton alleged that the council’s failure to accommodate her wishes amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment (Article 3), an unjustified interference with her private and family life (Article 8), and discrimination (Article 14) under the European Convention on Human Rights. The European Commission of Human Rights found her complaints inadmissible, concluding that the treatment did not reach the severity required for Article 3, and that Article 8 did not impose a positive obligation on authorities to provide accommodation of her choosing. No violation was found, and no remedies were awarded.

This case is significant as it illustrates the legal and practical barriers Roma and Traveller individuals face in preserving their cultural traditions, especially in the context of end-of-life dignity, at a time when the rights of these communities were only beginning to receive wider recognition in European human rights law.
